owner: xlog baseline — mainstream shorts conventions + pilot creator reference (LoL commentary style; subtitle-sync reference added v4)

criteria.name: hook_strength
criteria.description: The opening must stop the scroll immediately: cold-open on the highest-action / highest-emotion moment with no title card, logo, self-introduction, or pre-roll, and land the first caption line within the first ~0.5s. Two accepted hook forms: (a) an unresolved claim or question that only completes in the next line, or (b) a bold, complete thesis claim ('this champion is the strongest late-game top') stated over already-in-progress action that the footage immediately proves. For live-action narrative footage, a peak-emotion face plus visible physical evidence (bruise, grip, tears) beats a detail/object insert as the 0s frame. Judged over the first 3 seconds.

criteria.name: mainstream_convention
criteria.description: Follows proven, broadly appealing Shorts/Reels conventions for caption placement, structure, and readability. Safe beats experimental — except that the creator's reference establishes narration-subtitle-driven gameplay commentary as an accepted house form; do not penalize on their own either a centered vertical crop that keeps the game HUD readable or 16:9-in-9:16 letterboxing. Gameplay shots of 3–5s are acceptable, and expected, when each one carries new visible information and the cut lands on a sentence boundary.

criteria.name: instruction_fit
criteria.description: Faithfully realizes the user's free-form request (caption tone, effects, mood). When the brief asks for subtitles, near-every-beat captioning is expected and a run of silent shots is a real miss — but deliberate short caption gaps (0.5–1.5s) during narration pauses, in-game banners, or the peak beat are intentional craft, not a miss. Ignore this criterion (redistribute judgment) when no request was given.

criteria.name: pacing
criteria.description: No dead air and energy rising toward the payoff. Perceived pace is narration-led: subtitles swap exactly on spoken clause boundaries (each caption held ~2–4s) and cuts land on sentence boundaries with shots running ~3–5s, so text and picture turn over together. Caption/audio sync is the primary pacing lever — text that leads the audio or lingers past it is a defect even if the cut rhythm is good. Deliberate rhythm breaks (a mid-roll still interlude, one caption-free breath before the payoff) are welcome when they set up a payoff. Tighter cutting alone does not outrank a clearer, better-grounded arc.

criteria.name: narrative_clarity
criteria.description: One clear thread from hook to payoff; no confusing jumps. The strongest shape is question → clue → reveal: the hook poses a question or thesis, each following shot releases one new visible clue, and the payoff answers it with a concrete detail rather than restating the premise. Every caption must be anchored to something actually visible in the frame — inferred or atmospheric assertions the footage does not show are a clarity defect, not a stylistic choice. Silent visual interludes are fine when they restate the narration's point rather than introduce a new one.

criteria.name: moment_selection
criteria.description: The genuinely best raw moments were used, not filler. Prefer shots that contain concrete, readable evidence (faces at peak emotion, hands, marks, revealed names/objects, HUD gold/level/item state) over connective coverage such as low-angle feet, wide walking, or empty-space shots.

preferences: Open on frame one over already-in-progress action with the first caption inside 0.5 seconds — either a bold thesis claim the footage instantly proves or an unresolved claim that only completes in the next line — with no intro, logo, or self-introduction.

For live-action narrative footage, structure the edit as question → clue → reveal: hook on a peak-emotion face close-up that poses the question, release one new visible clue per shot, and pay it off with a concrete detail shot that answers it.
Caption only what is literally visible in the frame (a bruise, a hand gripping an arm, a name tattooed on skin); avoid interpretive or atmospheric lines that assert things the footage does not show.
Choose footage that literally demonstrates the sentence being narrated, and order clips chronologically (early game → late game) so the argument escalates toward the payoff.
Cut only on sentence or clause boundaries so every shot change coincides with a new narration line, keeping gameplay shots roughly 3–5 seconds.
Swap each subtitle exactly on the spoken clause boundary and hold it 2–4 seconds — never let text appear before the audio or linger past it.
Limit each caption to two lines of roughly 8–16 characters, breaking lines at natural grammatical phrase points instead of mid-phrase.

Burn captions as bold white text with a heavy dark outline or drop shadow, hard-cut in and out with no animation, centered in the lower third above the game HUD and never covering the minimap, item bar, or scoreboard.
Insert deliberate 0.5–1.5s caption gaps during narration pauses, whenever the game shows its own banner (kill, tower, level-up), and on the peak action beat so the on-screen event reads cleanly.
Pin a fixed subject anchor such as the champion or topic icon at top-center for the entire video as a constant identity cue.
Frame gameplay 9:16 either by cropping vertically with the champion centered or by letterboxing the 16:9 image, keeping the HUD readable and using any black bars as caption space.
When the brief asks for subtitles, keep a caption on nearly every beat and reserve silence for the planned gaps and the final loop cut.
Insert one silent full-bleed meme/still interlude around the 55–70% mark that visually restates the narration's joke, holding each still 2–3 seconds.
Join interlude stills with 0.5–1s dip-to-black fades rather than hard cuts, and drop all captions during the interlude so the image carries the gag.
End on a caption over a final decisive clip — a takeaway generalization or a short self-deprecating reaction — and fade out mid-play instead of using an outro card or CTA.
Avoid emojis and on-screen title cards.
notes: v4 — merged the pilot creator's reference short https://youtube.com/shorts/Zcw78KRcF9g?si=00S0zhk--Ss-X1pH (Korean LoL 'Dr. Mundo top' champion-guide short, ~56s, vertically cropped gameplay + voiceover). Creator note: '영상의 자막의 타이밍과 싱크가 잘 맞음. 그걸 학습' — the thing to learn is caption timing/sync, so pacing now names caption/audio sync as the primary pacing lever and treats early or lingering text as a defect. What the reference taught: cuts land on sentence/clause boundaries with ~3–5s shots; ~14 caption blocks over 56s (one text beat every ~3.5s), each held 2–4s and hard-cut with no animation; max two lines of ~8–16 chars broken at phrase boundaries; deliberate 0.5–1.5s blanks during pauses and over in-game banners; a fixed champion icon pinned top-center as an identity anchor; HUD deliberately left readable as evidence; frame-one thesis caption over mid-action with no intro; closing takeaway generalization instead of a CTA. Criterion edits made only where the reference contradicted v3: hook_strength now accepts a complete bold thesis claim (not just an unresolved claim); pacing dropped the 'long uncut takes + one line every 1–2s' model in favor of clause-synced swaps every 2–4s over 3–5s shots; mainstream_convention widened the acceptable shot length to 3–5s and now accepts centered vertical crop alongside letterboxing; instruction_fit clarifies that short deliberate caption gaps are craft, not a caption-density miss. Weights unchanged (single reference, sync-focused). Preferences: the old 'translucent plate' caption spec was replaced by the reference's heavy dark outline/drop shadow, the letterbox rule generalized to include vertical crop, and the two ending rules merged; six new rules added (clause-boundary cutting, clause-synced 2–4s captions, two-line/8–16-char limit, deliberate caption gaps, top-center subject anchor, footage-demonstrates-narration with chronological escalation). Live-action narrative rules from v3 retained unchanged since this reference did not exercise them.
